This is a well-known ethical dilemma in the therapy field, and most professional guidelines actually caution against a single counselor holding both roles precisely because of situations like this.

When a therapist sees a couple together and also sees one partner individually, they can end up holding a "secret" (like an affair) that creates a conflict of interest. To avoid this, many counselors establish a clear policy at the outset—often a "no secrets" policy, where information shared individually may be relevant to the couples work, or a strict confidentiality policy where individual sessions stay private. Others simply won't take on both roles at once.

If a therapist learns of infidelity and has no prior agreement, they generally can't just disclose it in a joint session without violating confidentiality. Instead, they'd typically work with the individual client to encourage disclosure themselves, or reconsider whether they can ethically continue the couples work.

If you're facing this personally, a consultation with a licensed clinician could help you sort through your specific situation.
